questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Git is a ________ version control system, meaning every clone holds the project's entire history, not just whatever the central server has.
questions.explain: Git is a distributed version control system: every developer's machine holds a full copy of the project's entire history, not just the current files. That's why Git works offline and why branching and merging are fast and cheap compared to older centralized systems like Subversion.

questions.prompt: A new teammate clones a repository onto a brand-new laptop and runs git commit for the first time. Git stops and complains that it doesn't know who they are. What's the actual fix, and why does it only need to happen once per machine?
options: Run git config --global user.name and git config --global user.email once — --global applies that identity to every repository on this machine, not just the current one
Run git config user.name and git config user.email inside every repository separately, since identity has to be set per project
Create a GitHub account first — Git reads the commit identity from whichever account is logged into GitHub Desktop
Add a name and email as a comment at the top of the first file committed
questions.explain: Git needs an identity to attach to every commit before it will let you commit at all. git config --global user.name/user.email writes that identity to ~/.gitconfig, which is exactly why --global makes it apply across every repository on that machine — you only set it once per machine, not once per project.

questions.prompt: A file moves through three places before it's part of the project's history. Put these actions in the order they actually happen.
items: Edit report.py in the working directory
Stage the change with git add report.py
Commit the staged change with git commit -m "Add quarterly totals"
See the new commit at the top of git log
questions.explain: Every tracked file moves working directory → staging area → repository. You edit in the working directory, git add moves that specific change into the staging area, git commit saves everything staged as a permanent snapshot, and only then does it actually show up in git log.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Git branches, per this course.
options: A branch is a lightweight, movable pointer to a commit — creating one doesn't copy any files
git switch -c new-branch and the older git checkout -b new-branch both create a branch and switch to it in one step
Every new branch starts as a full, separate copy of the project's files at the moment it's created
git branch -d deletes a branch safely only if its changes are already merged
Committing on a feature branch also moves main's pointer forward, since main is the default branch
questions.explain: A branch is just a movable pointer to a commit, not a file copy — that's exactly why branching is instant and cheap. switch -c and the older checkout -b both create-and-switch in one step. git branch -d refuses to delete a branch whose changes aren't merged yet, as a safety check. Committing on a feature branch only moves that branch's own pointer forward; main stays exactly where it was until something actually merges into it.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: when git rebase replays feature-login's commits onto main's current tip, those replayed commits get new ________ even though their code changes are identical to the originals — which is exactly why rebasing commits that have already been pushed and shared is dangerous.
questions.explain: Rebase doesn't move the original commits — it replays them as brand-new commit objects with new hashes, even though the actual code changes are the same. If those original commits were already pushed and someone else pulled them, rebasing creates a mismatch between your new history and their old one that's genuinely painful to untangle.

questions.prompt: main and feature-login have diverged — both have commits the other doesn't. While feature-login is checked out, you run git rebase main. What actually happens to the commits unique to feature-login?
options: They're replayed one at a time on top of main's current tip, producing new commits with new hashes but the same code changes
They're replayed one at a time on top of main's current tip, keeping their original commit hashes since the code changes themselves didn't change
A single new merge commit is created with both branch tips as parents, while every original commit on both branches stays untouched
They're discarded, and feature-login is reset to point at exactly the same commit as main
They're applied to main directly, and feature-login is deleted automatically once the rebase finishes
Each commit has to be cherry-picked individually with a separate git cherry-pick command before the rebase will continue
questions.distractorExplain: Option B keeps the right mental model — commits unique to feature-login get replayed on top of main's tip — but gets the one detail backwards: a replayed commit is a genuinely new commit object with a new hash, not the original commit relocated with its hash intact. That new-hash detail is exactly why rebasing commits someone else has already pulled creates a mismatch between their history and yours.
questions.explain: git rebase main takes the commits unique to the current branch and replays them, one at a time, on top of main's current tip — as if the branch had started there in the first place. Those replayed commits are new commit objects with new hashes, even though the code changes they contain are identical to the originals. Nothing is merged and no merge commit is created; the result is a clean, linear history.

questions.code:
<<<<<<< HEAD
greeting = "Hello there!"
=======
greeting = "Hi, welcome!"
>>>>>>> feature-login
questions.prompt: Git inserted this into greeting.py during a merge. Which statement correctly reads these markers?
options: The line between <<<<<<< HEAD and ======= is the version from the branch currently checked out; the line between ======= and >>>>>>> feature-login is the version coming from feature-login
The line between <<<<<<< HEAD and ======= is from feature-login; the line after ======= is from the branch currently checked out
Git has already chosen the HEAD version as correct; the feature-login version is shown only for reference and will be discarded automatically
This file can't be saved or committed until the markers are removed by running git merge --abort
questions.explain: HEAD always labels the version from the branch you're currently on; the section after ======= is labeled with the name of the branch being merged in — feature-login here. Nothing else in the file is touched, only the exact conflicting lines get these markers, and resolving means editing the file to its correct final content and removing the markers yourself — not running merge --abort, which cancels the merge entirely instead of resolving it.

questions.prompt: Match each merge-conflict term to what it actually means.
right: Marks one specific file's conflict as resolved, telling Git it's ready to be part of the merge commit
The label for the version of the conflicting lines from the branch you're currently on
Editing a conflicted file to its correct final content and removing the markers entirely
What happens when both branches changed the exact same lines of the exact same file in different ways
questions.explain: A merge conflict happens when both branches changed the same lines of the same file differently. Git labels the branch you're on as HEAD within the markers. Resolving means editing the file to its correct final content with the markers removed — not just picking one side. git add during a conflict marks that specific file as resolved, which is how git status knows a conflict is cleared.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the conventional (though not technically required) name for a repository's primary remote is ________.
questions.explain: A remote is just a named reference to a repository hosted elsewhere. Nothing forces the name origin, but it's the overwhelming convention — git clone sets it up automatically, and git remote add origin <url> is the standard way to attach it by hand.

questions.prompt: A developer already has a local repository from git init, with real commit history, and wants to connect it to a brand-new, empty GitHub repository. Which command should they use, and why is git clone the wrong choice here?
options: git remote add origin <url> — it attaches a remote to the existing local repo without downloading anything; git clone would instead try to download a repository, and the new GitHub repo is empty
git clone <url> — it's the only command that can connect a local repo to GitHub at all
git remote add origin <url> — it deletes the local repo's existing history and replaces it with GitHub's
git push origin main — pushing alone creates the remote connection with no prior setup needed
questions.explain: git remote add origin <url> attaches a remote to a repository you already have locally, without transferring anything yet — git push is still what actually sends commits there. git clone is for the opposite starting point: downloading an existing repository and setting up origin automatically. Running clone against an empty new GitHub repo wouldn't connect it to the existing local history at all.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about git fetch versus git pull, per this course.
options: git fetch downloads new commits from the remote and updates your local record of its branches, without touching your own working files or current branch
git pull does exactly what fetch does, then immediately merges (or, with --rebase, rebases) those changes into your current branch
git fetch automatically merges incoming changes into your current branch, just like git pull does
Running git fetch origin before pulling lets you preview what's incoming with something like git log main..origin/main before deciding what to do
git pull can never produce a merge conflict, since it only downloads changes
questions.explain: fetch only downloads and updates your local record of the remote's branches — it never touches your working files or merges anything. pull does the same download, then immediately merges (or rebases) into your current branch, which is exactly why it can surprise you with a conflict if you hadn't looked first. Fetching first, then previewing with a log or diff, is the safer habit this course recommends before deciding what to actually bring in.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of this course's recommended 'fetch first' habit in order, for catching a branch up safely after time away.
items: git fetch origin — download what's new, with no risk to your current branch
git log main..origin/main — preview exactly what's incoming before touching anything
git pull origin main — now actually bring the previewed changes in
questions.explain: Fetching first costs nothing and carries no risk, since it never touches your working files. Previewing what's incoming with a log (or diff) lets you see what you're about to merge before you commit to it. Only then does pull actually bring those changes into your current branch.

questions.prompt: A pull request changes 40 files across six unrelated concerns in one shot. Per this course, what's the real problem with this, and what should the author do differently?
options: It's genuinely hard to review well — reviewers either rubber-stamp it or spend hours on it; splitting it into several focused PRs, one coherent change each, is faster to review and far easier to revert cleanly
There's no real problem — GitHub has no limit on PR size, so a larger PR is just as easy to review as a small one
The PR should be closed and the same 40 files committed directly to main instead, skipping review entirely
The only fix is deleting some of the 40 files so the PR looks smaller, even if the functionality still depends on them
questions.explain: A pull request focused on one coherent change is faster to review, faster to merge, and far easier to revert cleanly if something's wrong with it — the same discipline the staging area teaches at the commit level, applied at the PR level. A 40-file, six-concern PR tends to get either rubber-stamped or stuck in review for hours.

questions.prompt: Match each code review action to what it actually does.
right: Explicitly blocks the merge until whatever was flagged is addressed
Feedback with no formal verdict — doesn't block or approve the merge
Tracks which files in a large diff you've already looked at, and resets if the author pushes new commits to one
Signals you're satisfied with the changes — often required before the merge button unlocks, depending on branch protection
questions.explain: Comment leaves feedback with no formal verdict. Approve signals satisfaction and, depending on branch protection rules, may be required before merging unlocks. Request changes explicitly blocks the merge until it's addressed. The Viewed checkbox just tracks your own progress through a large diff, and deliberately resets if the author pushes new commits to a file you'd already checked off.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: writing "________ #42" in a pull request's description (Closes or Fixes both work) links it to that issue, and merging the PR automatically closes it.
questions.explain: Writing a phrase like Closes #42 or Fixes #42 in a pull request's description links it to that issue — merging the PR automatically closes the issue, which is the connective tissue between 'here's the problem' and 'here's the fix.'

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Git Flow versus trunk-based development, per this course.
options: Git Flow uses several long-lived branch types — main, develop, feature/*, release/*, hotfix/* — each with a specific job
Trunk-based development has one long-lived branch, with everyone's feature branches merging back within a day or two
Trunk-based teams often use feature flags to ship unfinished code to main (and even production) while keeping it switched off until it's ready
Git Flow is the better fit for a SaaS product deploying to production multiple times a day
A release/* branch in Git Flow is meant to accept new feature work right up until release
questions.explain: Git Flow's structure is built around main, develop, feature/*, release/*, and hotfix/* branches, suited to scheduled, versioned releases. Trunk-based development instead keeps one long-lived branch and merges short-lived feature branches back frequently, relying on feature flags to hide unfinished work rather than letting it live on a branch indefinitely. A SaaS product shipping many times a day is the classic trunk-based case, not Git Flow's — and a release/* branch is explicitly bug-fixes-only, not a place for new features.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of a Git Flow release, exactly as this course walks through it, in the correct order.
items: Branch release/2.4.0 off develop, accepting only bug fixes from this point on
Once the release branch is stable, merge it into main
Tag the commit on main as the release (e.g. v2.4.0)
Merge the same release branch into develop so its bug fixes aren't lost there
questions.explain: A release branch forks from develop and, from that point on, takes only bug fixes — no new features. Once it's stable it merges into main, which gets tagged as the actual release point. The same release branch is then also merged back into develop, so none of its bug fixes are lost on that side — missing this last step is exactly how develop and main drift out of sync.

questions.prompt: A contributor wants to propose a change to a popular open-source repository they have no write access to. What should they do, and how is this actually different from git clone?
options: Fork the repository on GitHub first — this creates a complete, independent copy under their own account with full push access, which they then clone locally; git clone alone would still point at the same original repository they can't push to
Run git clone on the original repository, then push a branch directly to it — clone grants write access automatically to anyone who runs it
Ask the maintainers to add them as a collaborator before doing anything else; there is no other way to contribute
Fork and clone are the same operation under a different name — forking just happens on GitHub's website instead of the command line
questions.explain: git clone downloads a copy of a repository, but it's still the same remote repository on GitHub — you still need write access to push to it. Forking creates a genuinely separate repository on GitHub itself, fully owned by the contributor, which they then clone locally to work on. That's exactly how someone without any write access can still propose changes, via a pull request comparing across forks.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: in a cross-fork pull request, the ________ is the original repository and branch you want your change merged into — the head is your fork and the branch holding your proposed commits.
questions.explain: GitHub's cross-fork comparison asks for both sides explicitly: the base is the original project's repository and branch, and the head is your fork and your branch. It's easy to get these backwards the first time.

questions.code:
$ git log -S "MAX_RETRIES" --oneline
e4c8a91 Lower retry ceiling after incident review
b2f0d73 Add exponential backoff with configurable retry limit
questions.prompt: MAX_RETRIES no longer exists anywhere in the current codebase, and you need to find the commit that removed it. Why can't git blame on the current file answer this, and what's the right tool instead?
options: git blame only annotates lines that currently exist in the file — a deleted line has nothing left to blame; git log -S "MAX_RETRIES" searches every commit's diff for that string, including the commit that removed it
git blame already searches deleted lines automatically — the right fix is just adding the --follow flag
git log -p walks every commit ever made to the repository, not just ones touching that string, so it's strictly better than git log -S here
Nothing in Git can find when a deleted piece of code was removed; this requires checking out every past commit manually and comparing by hand
questions.explain: git blame annotates the lines a file currently has — a removed line simply isn't there to annotate anymore. git log -S (the 'pickaxe') searches every commit's actual diff for a string, finding commits that added or removed it, which is exactly what's needed once the code in question no longer exists in the current file.

questions.prompt: Match each tags-and-releases term to what it actually is.
right: Pushes every tag that exists locally to the remote in one command
Just a name pointing at a commit, with no extra metadata stored
Wraps an existing tag with release notes, downloadable source archives, and optionally built artifacts
A real Git object storing a message, tagger name, date, and optionally a GPG signature
questions.explain: A lightweight tag is just a name pointing at a commit. An annotated tag is a full Git object with a message, tagger, date, and optional signature — the one to actually use for a release. git push origin --tags sends every local tag to the remote at once. A GitHub Release then wraps an existing tag with notes and optional downloadable artifacts.

questions.prompt: A .pem file was committed to a repository three weeks ago. Today, the team adds *.pem to .gitignore and runs git rm --cached on the file. Is the original key now safe?
options: No — the key is still sitting in every previous commit, clone, and fork's history; it needs to be rotated, and the history itself would need to be rewritten to actually remove it
Yes — .gitignore combined with git rm --cached fully erases the file from every past commit automatically
Yes, as long as the repository is set to private after making this change
No, but only because .gitignore patterns need a leading slash to take effect — the fix is adding /*.pem instead
questions.explain: .gitignore only prevents future commits of a file, and git rm --cached only stops tracking it going forward — neither touches the commits that already exist. The key is still recoverable from history with something like git log -p until the history itself is rewritten (a separate, more invasive operation), which is why the real fix for an already-committed secret is rotating it, not just adding a pattern.

questions.prompt: A team's pipeline automatically builds and tests every change, and automatically packages a passing change as release-ready — but an engineer still has to click a button before it actually reaches production. Which practice does this describe, and what's the one-word difference from the practice most often confused with it?
options: Continuous Delivery — every change that passes CI is made release-ready automatically, but a human still approves the actual release; Continuous Deployment removes that approval step and deploys automatically

Continuous Deployment — every change that passes CI is made release-ready automatically, but a human still approves the actual release; Continuous Delivery removes that approval step and deploys automatically
Continuous Integration — this is simply CI with a manual approval step bolted on, unrelated to delivery or deployment
Continuous Delivery — functionally identical to Continuous Deployment, since both still package the code the same way before release
Continuous Deployment — the manual approval step described only exists in regulated industries and isn't a real part of the practice
Continuous Delivery — this pipeline is actually broken, since any real CI/CD pipeline must deploy straight to production automatically
questions.distractorExplain: Option B describes the right mechanics — automatic release-readiness with a manual approval gate — but swaps which term it belongs to. Continuous Delivery is the one that keeps the human approval step; Continuous Deployment is specifically the practice that removes it. Getting the two names backwards is the single most common mix-up with this pair of terms.
questions.explain: Continuous Delivery means every change that passes CI is automatically packaged and made release-ready, but a human still clicks the button to actually ship it — release timing stays a deliberate decision. Continuous Deployment removes that last click entirely: every passing change deploys straight to production with no manual approval step at all. The scenario described — automatic readiness, manual release — is Continuous Delivery.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about CI/CD, per this course.
options: Continuous Integration automatically builds and tests every change on every push or pull request, catching a broken build while it's still fresh
CI/CD only applies to web applications and backend services, not data pipelines
A dbt project running dbt run and dbt test before promoting models to a production schema is CI/CD applied to a data pipeline, using the same underlying mechanism
Continuous Deployment deploys every change that passes CI straight to production automatically, with no human approval step
CI, Continuous Delivery, and Continuous Deployment are three unrelated terms that happen to get bundled together under one buzzword
questions.explain: CI automates build-and-test on every push or PR, catching problems while they're still one person's fresh change. The same build-verify-release shape applies well beyond web apps — a dbt project's run-then-test-then-promote cycle is CI/CD using the identical underlying mechanism. Continuous Deployment specifically is the stage that removes the manual approval and deploys automatically. The three terms aren't unrelated — they're a chain, each stage automating more than the one before it.

questions.code:
name: Explore GitHub Actions
on: [push]
jobs:
  explore:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo "This job was triggered by a push."
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: echo "The repository has been cloned to the runner."
questions.prompt: Put these events in the order they actually happen once this workflow file is committed and pushed to its repository.
items: The YAML file is committed to .github/workflows/ and pushed — no separate registration step is needed anywhere in GitHub's settings
The push event triggers a new run automatically
The run appears on the repository's Actions tab
Clicking into the job expands each step, in the order it ran, with its own timing and output
questions.explain: GitHub scans .github/workflows/ automatically — committing a file there is the entire setup. Once pushed, the on: [push] trigger fires a run with no manual step. Every run, across every workflow file, shows up on the Actions tab, and clicking into the job expands its steps in the order they actually executed, each with its own duration — exactly where you'd go to debug a failure.

questions.prompt: A repository's test workflow runs on every push and pull request, but the repository has no branch protection rules configured. A PR's commit shows a red X for a failing test. What actually happens if someone clicks the PR's Merge button anyway?
options: The PR merges normally — a failing status check is only a visual indicator by default; nothing blocks the merge unless a branch protection rule marks that check as required
GitHub refuses to merge any PR with a failing check, regardless of branch protection settings
The merge button is disabled automatically the moment any workflow run fails, with no configuration needed
The PR merges, but GitHub automatically reverts it a few minutes later once it detects the failing check
questions.explain: By default, a failing status check is only a red X next to the PR — a visual indicator, not an enforced rule. Nothing actually stops a merge unless the repository has a branch protection rule marking that specific check as required. Without that rule configured, the gap between 'someone will notice and not merge' and an actual enforced block is real, and it's exactly what required status checks exist to close.

questions.code:
deploy:
  needs: build-and-test
  if: github.event_name == 'push' && github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
  runs-on: ubuntu-latest
  steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v4
    - run: npm run deploy
questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the keyword ________ in this job (set to github.event_name == 'push' && github.ref == 'refs/heads/main') is what actually gates this job so it only runs on a real merge to main, never on an open pull request.
questions.explain: The if condition is evaluated before the job runs. Here it only evaluates true when the event is a push (not a pull_request) and the ref is literally refs/heads/main — in other words, only on a real merge commit landing on main, never on an open PR and never on a push to some other branch.

questions.prompt: Per the capstone brief, select every requirement a complete capstone repository must actually satisfy.
options: A commit history with meaningful, individually reviewable commits, including at least one deliberate merge conflict that was actually resolved
A reviewed pull request with a real description, including at least one inline comment addressed with a follow-up commit
A written note stating whether the project uses Git Flow or trunk-based development, plus an annotated tag marking a release point
A .github/workflows/ file that runs the project's real tests (or a meaningful validation step) on every push and PR, plus a separate job gated to real merges only
At least three different programming languages used in the project, to demonstrate range
Dynamic task scheduling or a message queue wired into the repository's CI pipeline
questions.explain: The brief's five numbered sections ask for real reviewable history with a genuinely resolved merge conflict, a reviewed PR with an addressed inline comment, a branching-strategy note plus an annotated release tag, a .gitignore matching the project with no secrets in history, and a real CI/CD workflow with a job gated to actual merges. Nothing in the brief asks for multiple languages or a message queue — those aren't capstone requirements at all.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of this course's recommended capstone walkthrough order in sequence, as described in the wrap-up lesson.
items: Show the commit graph and branch history, proving a real feature branch merged through a real pull request
Show the pull request itself — the description, plus the inline review comment addressed with a follow-up commit
Pull up the resolved merge conflict and explain what it actually was and why that version was kept
Show the Actions tab's real run history, and explain the deploy job's condition for why it only fires on a real merge
Show the release tag, along with the written reasoning for the branching strategy chosen
questions.explain: The recommended order builds credibility step by step: the commit graph and branch history first proves the workflow is real, then the PR itself demonstrates real review given and received, then the resolved conflict shows a real problem actually handled, then the Actions tab proves CI/CD is real and correctly gated, and finally the release tag ties it together with the reasoning behind the branching choice.

questions.prompt: In an interview, you're asked: 'What stops your deploy job from running on every single push?' Based on the capstone project, what's the correct answer?
options: The job's if condition, checking that github.event_name is push (not pull_request) and github.ref is literally refs/heads/main — so it only evaluates true on a real merge to main
GitHub Actions deploy jobs are hard-coded to only run once a day, regardless of how many pushes happen
Branch protection rules block the deploy job automatically; the if condition is just a formality
Nothing stops it — the deploy job is expected to run on every single push, including to feature branches
questions.explain: The deploy job's if condition is what actually gates it: it only evaluates true when the event is a push (not a pull_request) and the ref is refs/heads/main. That's what makes it fire only on a real merge to main — not branch protection rules, which govern merging, not which Actions jobs execute.
